en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 5.
The Chapter on Leather (Cammakkhandhaka)
1. The Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha, exercised sovereign power and ruled over eighty thousand villages.
Now at that time in Campā there was a son of a merchant named Soṇa Koḷivisa, who was very delicate.
Hair had grown on the soles of his feet.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha, having assembled those eighty thousand village headmen for some business, sent a messenger to Soṇa Koḷivisa, saying:
“Let Soṇa come; I wish for Soṇa to come.
Then Soṇa Koḷivisa’s parents said this to him:
“Dear Soṇa, the king wishes to see your feet.”
"Do not, dear Soṇa, extend your feet toward where the king is.
Sit cross-legged in front of the king.
When you are seated, the king will see your feet."
Then they brought Soṇa Koḷivisa in a palanquin.
Then Soṇa Koḷivisa approached King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha; having approached, he paid homage to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha and sat down cross-legged before the king.
King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha saw that hair had grown on the soles of Soṇa Koḷivisa’s feet.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having instructed those eighty thousand village headmen on matters pertaining to the present life, dismissed them, saying:
"Indeed, sirs, you have been instructed by me on matters pertaining to the present life;
go, attend upon that Blessed One."
"Therefore, the Blessed One will instruct us regarding the welfare of the future life.
Then those eighty thousand village headmen approached Mount Vulture Peak.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāgata was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Then those eighty thousand village headmen approached the Venerable Sāgata; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Sāgata:
"Venerable sir, these eighty thousand village headmen have come here desiring to see the Blessed One;
it would be well, venerable sir, if we might obtain a sight of the Blessed One."
“In that case, venerable sirs, remain right here for a moment while I inform the Blessed One.

Then the Venerable Sāgata, in front of those eighty thousand village headmen who were looking on, sank down into the stone slab and emerged in front of the Blessed One, and he said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these eighty thousand village headmen have come here to see the Blessed One.”
“Venerable sir, please do as you deem fit now.
“In that case, Sāgata, prepare a seat in the shade of the dwelling.
“Very well, venerable sir,” he replied.

Having assented to the Blessed One, the Venerable Sāgata took a bench, submerged himself in front of the Blessed One, and then, while those eighty thousand village headmen were looking on, emerged from a water pipe. He then prepared a seat in the shade of the monastery.
Then the Blessed One came out from the monastery and sat down on the seat prepared in the shade of the monastery.
Then those eighty thousand village headmen approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Then those eighty thousand village headmen directed their attention toward the Venerable Sāgata alone, and not so much toward the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those eighty thousand village headmen, addressed the Venerable Sāgata:
“In that case, Sāgata, show us even more, further than this, a superhuman feat of psychic power.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Sāgata replied to the Blessed One.
Having assented, he rose up into the air and, while in the sky, in the firmament, he walked back and forth, stood, sat down, and lay down; he emitted smoke and burst into flames, and then vanished.

Then the Venerable Sāgata, having displayed various kinds of superhuman states and miracles of psychic power in the open sky, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher;
I am a disciple.”
“The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir;
I am his disciple.
Then those eighty thousand village headmen exclaimed, “It is wonderful, indeed! It is marvelous, indeed!”

"Even a disciple shall be so powerful and so majestic; oh, how great must the Teacher be! they thought, directing their attention toward the Blessed One alone, and not likewise toward the Venerable Sāgata.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thoughts arising in the minds of those eighty thousand village headmen, delivered a gradual discourse, namely:
a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that his mind was ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and serene, he then set forth that Dhamma exposition which is uniquely proclaimed by Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye;
In the same way, for those eighty thousand village headmen, the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye arose in that very seat:
"Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.

Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and fathomed the Dharma; having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence, and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [so it has been done by the Blessed One].”
In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, we go for refuge to the Blessed One,
and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

“May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Then it occurred to Soṇa Koḷivisa: “The Blessed One has accepted me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. What if I were now to go forth?”
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life in its complete fullness, in its utter purity, polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?”
Then those eighty thousand village headmen, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, departed.
Not long after those eighty thousand village headmen had left, Soṇa Koḷivisa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, Soṇa Koḷivisa said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, in its total purity, polished like a conch shell.
Venerable sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.
May the Blessed One grant me the going-forth.”
Soṇa Koḷivisa received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
Not long after his ordination, the Venerable Soṇa was dwelling in the Cool Grove.
As he walked back and forth with over-exerted energy, his feet were split.
The walking path was covered with blood, just like a slaughterhouse for cattle.
Then, as the Venerable Soṇa was dwelling in seclusion and retreat, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Of those disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused, I am one of them."
"And yet, my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Moreover, there is wealth in my family;
it is possible for me both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds."
“What if I were to turn back to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Venerable Soṇa’s mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— vanished from Vulture Peak Mountain and reappeared in the Cool Grove.
Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings together with a number of bhikkhus, approached the place where the Venerable Soṇa was walking.
The Blessed One saw that the Venerable Soṇa’s walkway was covered with blood, as if it were a slaughterhouse for cattle. Having seen this, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, whose walkway is this, covered with blood, like a slaughterhouse for cattle?”
“Venerable sir, while the Venerable Soṇa was walking back and forth with over-exerted energy, his feet were split open.
This walkway of his is covered in blood, as if it were a slaughterhouse for cattle.
Then the Blessed One went to the Venerable Soṇa’s dwelling, and having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Soṇa also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Soṇa was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Soṇa, did not such a reflection arise in your mind when you had gone into seclusion and were dwelling in solitude?”
‘Of those disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused, I am one of them.
Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
However, there is wealth in my family.’
“It is possible both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.
What if I were to return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?
“So be it, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, Soṇa, were you skilled formerly, when you were a householder, in the tuning of the strings of a lute?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Soṇa, when the strings of your lute were too tight, was your lute at that time capable of being played and did it produce sound? “No, venerable sir.”
“No, Bhante.
“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute are too loose, does your lute at that time produce sound or remain functional?
“No, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Soṇa, when the strings of your lute are neither too tight nor too loose, but are settled on even tension, would your lute at that time produce sound, or would it be serviceable?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Soṇa, over-exerted energy leads to restlessness, and overly slack energy leads to laziness.”
"Therefore, Soṇa, resolve upon evenness of energy, penetrate the evenness of the faculties, and seize the sign therein.
"Yes, venerable sir," the Venerable Soṇa replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Soṇa with this instruction—just as a strong man might...
Just as one might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm, even so,
having vanished from the presence of the Venerable Soṇa in the Cool Grove, he reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then, after some time,
the Venerable Soṇa resolved upon the balance of energy, penetrated the balance of the faculties, and grasped the sign therein.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Soṇa, in no long time,

realized for himself through direct knowledge and attained, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Soṇa became one of the arahants.
Then, when the Venerable Soṇa had attained arahantship, this thought occurred to him:
“What if I were now to declare final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One?
Then the Venerable Soṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Soṇa said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through final knowledge, is intent upon six things:
he is intent upon renunciation, intent upon seclusion, intent upon non-affliction, intent upon the destruction of clinging, intent upon the destruction of craving, and intent upon non-delusion.
Now, venerable sir, it might occur to some venerable one here:”
‘Surely this venerable one is intent on renunciation only by relying on mere faith’— but, Bhante, it should not be viewed in that way.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done and perceives no further task for himself,
is intent on renunciation because he is free from lust through the destruction of lust, and free from hatred through the destruction of hatred.
Because he is free from hatred, he is intent on renunciation; because delusion has been destroyed and he is free from delusion, he is intent on renunciation.
Yet, venerable sir, it might occur to some venerable one here:
‘Surely this venerable one is intent on seclusion because he desires gain, honor, and fame.’
But this, venerable sir, should not be viewed in such a way.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done and perceives no further task for himself,
is intent upon seclusion because he is free from lust through the destruction of lust, and free from hatred through the destruction of hatred.
Because he is free from hatred, he is intent upon seclusion; because he has destroyed delusion and is free from delusion, he is intent upon seclusion.
Now, venerable sir, it might occur to some venerable one here:
"Surely this venerable one is intent upon non-affliction because he returns to the core of the attachment to rules and observances."
But this, venerable sir, should not be viewed in such a way.

A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done and perceives no further task for himself, is—through the destruction of lust and being free from lust—devoted to non-affliction; through the destruction of hatred... [and] through the destruction of delusion... [he is devoted to non-affliction].
Because he is free from hatred, he is intent on non-affliction; because he is free from delusion through the destruction of delusion, he is intent on non-affliction.

Because he is free from lust through the destruction of lust, he is intent on the destruction of clinging; because he is free from hatred through the destruction of hatred, he is intent on the destruction of clinging; because he is free from delusion through the destruction of delusion, he is intent on the destruction of clinging.

Through the destruction of lust, by being free from lust, he is intent upon the destruction of craving; through the destruction of hatred, by being free from hatred, he is intent upon the destruction of craving; through the destruction of delusion, by being free from delusion, he is intent upon the destruction of craving.

Through the destruction of lust, by being free from lust, he is intent upon non-delusion; through the destruction of hatred, by being free from hatred, he is intent upon non-delusion; through the destruction of delusion, by being free from delusion, he is intent upon non-delusion.
"Venerable sir, when the mind of a bhikkhu is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, they do not obsess his mind.
His mind remains unadulterated, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
Even if powerful sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on for the other senses]..."
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body...
When mental phenomena come into the range of the mind, they do not overwhelm his consciousness;
his consciousness remains unmixed, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.

Just as, venerable sir, a solid rock mountain—without cracks, without hollows, a single mass—if a violent storm of wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would neither tremble, nor shake, nor quiver;
Even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the western direction... [and so on] ...even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the northern direction...
[and so on] ...even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the southern direction, it would not shake, it would not tremble, and it would not quiver.
In the same way, Bhante, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, they do not overwhelm his mind;
his mind remains unadulterated, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
Even if powerful sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on].
Odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body …
“Mental phenomena cognizable by the mind come into the range of his mind, yet they do not overwhelm his consciousness;
his consciousness remains unmixed, established, attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
Thus it is for one who is intent upon renunciation.
And solitude of mind;
for one intent on non-affliction and the destruction of clinging.
For one intent on the destruction of craving,
with a mind free from delusion,
having seen the arising of the sense-bases—
The mind is rightly liberated.
For that bhikkhu who is rightly liberated and whose mind is at peace:
For him there is no further accumulation;
nothing more remains to be done.
Like a solid mass of rock, he stands firm.
It is not stirred by the wind;
even so are forms, tastes, sounds,
smells, and tangibles in their entirety.
Desirable things and undesirable things do not cause trembling in the Tathāgata;
his mind is steadfast and fully liberated.
"And we shall look after her. 2.
The Prohibition Against Double-Layered Sandals, etc.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In this way, monks, sons of good family declare their final knowledge; the meaning is stated, yet the self is not brought forward.
Yet here some foolish men, it seems, declare their final knowledge with a smirk, and they later fall into distress.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Soṇa:
“Sonā, you are delicate.
I allow you, Sonā, sandals with a single layer of leather.
“Venerable sir, I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, having renounced eighty cartloads of gold and a troop of seven elephants.”
"But, venerable sir, if I were to wear sandals with single-layered soles, there would be those who would say of me:
'Soṇa Koḷivisa, having renounced eighty cartloads of gold and a troop of seven elephants, went forth from the home life into homelessness;
yet now he is attached to sandals with single-layered soles.'"
“If the Blessed One permits the Saṅgha of bhikkhus [to use it], I too shall use it;
if the Blessed One does not permit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I too shall not use it.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, sandals with a single layer of leather.
Monks, sandals with double layers of leather must not be worn.
Sandals with triple layers of leather must not be worn.”
“Sandalwood slippers with various colored straps must not be worn.
Whoever should wear them commits an offense of wrong-doing.
3. Prohibition of entirely blue and other [colored] [slippers].
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore sandals that were entirely blue … they wore sandals that were entirely yellow … they wore sandals that were entirely red …
They wear sandals that are entirely madder-red;
they wear sandals that are entirely black;
they wear sandals that are entirely dyed with mahāraṅga.
They wore sandals entirely dyed with red lac.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, sandals that are entirely blue should not be worn...
sandals that are entirely yellow should not be worn, sandals that are entirely red should not be worn, sandals that are entirely madder-colored should not be worn.”
“Sandals should be worn; sandals that are entirely black should not be worn; sandals that are entirely dyed with mahāraṅga should not be worn;
sandals that are entirely dyed with mahānāma should not be worn.
Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore sandals with blue straps;
they wore sandals with yellow straps; they wore sandals with red straps; they wore sandals with madder-red straps;
they wore sandals with black straps; they wore sandals with straps dyed with a deep color.
They wear them; they wear sandals with red straps.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying, "It is just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, sandals with blue straps must not be worn; ... pe ... sandals with yellow straps must not be worn;
sandals with red straps must not be worn; sandals with madder-red straps must not be worn.”
They should be worn; sandals with black straps must not be worn; sandals with straps dyed with mahāraṅga must not be worn; sandals with straps dyed with mahānāma must not be worn.
Whoever should wear them commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore sandals with heel-protectors;
they wore sandals with enclosed heels, sandals with leather covers, sandals stuffed with cotton,
sandals with partridge-feather linings, and sandals with ram-horn attachments.
They wore sandals made of goat horns, sandals with scorpion tails, sandals woven with peacock feathers, and variegated sandals.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, sandals bound with leather thongs must not be worn … [as before] …”
One should not wear sandals with enclosed tops; one should not wear sandals with leather covers; one should not wear sandals stuffed with cotton;
one should not wear sandals made of partridge feathers; one should not wear sandals bound with the horns of rams;
one should not wear sandals bound with the horns of goats; one should not wear sandals with scorpion-shaped ornaments.
“Sandals should be worn; sandals woven with peacock feathers should not be worn; variegated sandals should not be worn.
Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were wearing sandals trimmed with lion skins.
...pe... they wear sandals lined with tiger-skin, they wear sandals lined with leopard-skin,
they wear sandals lined with deerskin, they wear sandals lined with otter-skin,
they wear sandals lined with cat-skin, they wear sandals lined with black-skin.
They wore sandals made of leather with fur linings.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, sandals trimmed with lion skins should not be worn...
sandals trimmed with tiger skins should not be worn; sandals trimmed with leopard skins should not be worn.”
One should not wear sandals made from the skin of a black antelope,
nor sandals made from the skin of a water buffalo, nor sandals made from the skin of a cat, nor sandals made from the skin of a black dog,
nor sandals made from the skin of a jackal.
Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

4. The Allowance of Sandals with Straps Removed One Over Another Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms, with a certain bhikkhu as his attendant.
Then that bhikkhu, limping, followed closely behind the Blessed One.
A certain lay follower, having put on sandals with multiple layers of leather, saw the Blessed One coming from afar;
seeing him, he put on his sandals and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he went to where that bhikkhu was.
Having approached and paid homage to that bhikkhu, he said this:
"Venerable sir, why does the master limp?
"My feet are cracked, friend," he replied.
“Here, venerable sir, are sandals.
“Enough, friend; the Blessed One has prohibited sandals with multiple layers of leather.
“Take these sandals, bhikkhu.”
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, sandals with multiple layers of leather that have been worn out.
But, bhikkhus, new sandals with multiple layers of leather must not be worn.”
“Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth in the open air without sandals.
“The Teacher is walking without sandals,” thinking thus,
the elder bhikkhus also walked without sandals.
While the Teacher was walking without sandals and the elder bhikkhus were also walking without sandals, the group-of-six bhikkhus walked with sandals on.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these bhikkhus of the group of six walk with sandals on while the Teacher is walking without sandals, and while the elder bhikkhus are also walking without sandals?
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as above].

“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks, while the Teacher was walking up and down without sandals and while the elder monks were also walking up and down without sandals, walked up and down wearing sandals?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How, monks, can those foolish men, while the Teacher is walking up and down without sandals and while the elder monks are also walking up and down without sandals, walk up and down wearing sandals?
Monks, even householders dressed in white wear their clothes for the sake of a craft that provides a livelihood, yet they dwell with respect, deference, and harmonious conduct toward their teachers.
It would have been fitting, monks, for you who have gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya to do so.”
"You may dwell without respect, without deference, and with conduct inconsistent with the Dhamma toward your teachers, those who act as teachers, your preceptors, and those who act as preceptors.
This, monks, does not lead to the inspiration of the uninspired... Having rebuked them... [and so forth].
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, when teachers or those who are merely teachers, or preceptors or those who are merely preceptors, are walking up and down without sandals, one must not walk up and down wearing sandals.
Whoever should so walk commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
“Monks, sandals must not be worn within the monastery precincts.
Whoever should wear them commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain monk suffered from a foot ailment.
The monks, having taken hold of him, carried him out even for the sake of defecating or urinating.
While wandering about inspecting the lodgings, the Blessed One saw those monks taking hold of that monk and carrying him out even for the sake of defecating or urinating;
having seen this, he approached those monks, and having approached, [he stood there].
He said to those bhikkhus,
“Bhikkhus, what is this illness of that bhikkhu?
“Venerable sir, this venerable one has an ailment of corns on his feet.”
“Having taken hold of this, we shall discharge both feces and urine.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to wear sandals if your feet are painful, or if your feet are cracked, or if you have the affliction of corns on the feet.”
Now at that time, monks were climbing onto beds and benches with unwashed feet,
and their robes and lodgings became soiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to wear sandals with the thought: ‘Now I shall mount a bed or a chair.
Now at that time, monks going to the Uposatha hall or to a meeting at night stepped on stumps or thorns in the darkness; their feet became painful.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to wear sandals within the monastery grounds, as well as a torch, a lamp,
and a walking stick. Now at that time, on the occasion of the dawn of the night, the group of six monks rose and put on wooden sandals.
Having climbed up, they walked back and forth in the open air, making loud noises, great clamor, and clattering sounds,
engaging in various kinds of worldly talk,
such as talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, and talk of food.
talk about drinks, talk about clothes, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about scents, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages,
talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about countries, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells,
talk about the dead, talk about various matters, and talk about worldly speculation.

[They engage in] talk about the ocean, or talk concerning "thus it was" and "thus it will be"; they kill even insects by treading upon them, and they cause even monks to fall away from concentration. Those monks who have few desires... [and so on]... they criticize, grumble, and spread it about: ... [text omitted for brevity] ... "Friends, how can these wanderers of other sects engage in talk about kings, thieves, and ministers; talk about armies, threats, and wars; talk about food, drink, clothes, and beds; talk about garlands and perfumes; talk about relatives, vehicles, villages, towns, cities, and countries; talk about women and heroes; street talk and talk at the well; talk about the deceased; miscellaneous talk; talk about 'how it was' and 'how it will be'; and how they kill even insects by treading upon them and cause even monks to fall away from concentration? The Fifth Chapter on Leather.
Its summary verse:
The King of Magadha, Soṇa,
and the lord of eighty thousand.
Sāgata, on Vulture Peak,
displayed many further [powers].
Those who had broken their resolve regarding the going-forth were restored.
A one-sided lute;
blue, yellow, red,
madder-colored, and even black.
Mahāraṅga and Mahānāma,
Vaddhikā and Paṭikkhipi,
Khalakā and Puṭapāli.
Cotton, partridge, and goat hair; scorpions,
peacock-patterned cloth,
and those made from lion, tiger, and leopard skins.
A deer-skin rug, a cat,
a black and white partridge, a worn-out sandal,
a cracked sandal, and a thorn.
The *dhotakhāṇu* and the *khaṭakhaṭā*;
and likewise the *tāla*, *veḷu*, and *tiṇa*, as well as the *muñja*, *pabbaja*, and *hintāla*.
Like lotus-wool and gold,
silver, gems, and beryl;
crystal, bronze, and glass—
Tipu, lead, and copper;
a cow, a vehicle, and one who is ill;
a palanquin carried by men.
Large hides are for couches,
and goat-skins are for the wicked;
leather straps are for householders.
Entering [the city],
the sick Mahākaccāyana and Soṇa recited the Aṭṭhakavagga with a resonant voice.
He authorized full ordination by means of five qualities,
and the possession of the various virtues and constant mindfulness;
he also authorized the use of leather mats for spreading.
It was not yet even worth counting;
the Leader gave five boons to me, to the Elder Soṇa.
In this Khandhaka, there are sixty-three cases.
